Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette: Amir remembered the hotel ballroom as a blur of polished marble and low jazz, the night of the regional therapy conference bleeding into an unmarked elevator ride. The man who cornered him against the service corridor did not speak much; he just pressed a heavy, familiar blend of sandalwood and amber cologne into Amir's face, the scent so thick it felt like wool stuffed in his nose. When Amir tried to push him away, a sharp, twisting pain bloomed across his right ribs, a somatic anchor that would never truly fade. The forced sexual contact lasted only minutes, but it left a hollow, burning awareness in his pelvis that turned every subsequent moment of physical closeness into a trap, making the olfactory, somatic, and intimate cues he later encountered feel inescapably tied to that original violation. In the weeks that followed, the rehabilitation clinic where Amir worked as a physical therapist became a minefield. When a senior colleague leaned over his desk to discuss a treatment plan, wearing a similar citrus-and-woods fragrance, Amir's chest tightened until he had to excuse himself to the restroom. The heavy cologne and the familiar ache in his ribs did not just remind him of the night he was violated; they confirmed his worsening belief that he could never rely on himself to stay safe, that his body was permanently marked with shame, and that he would never feel normal emotions again. That conviction did not remain passive. It fed directly into a state of perpetual alarm, his shoulders hiking to his ears the moment a patient's gurney rolled too quickly down the hall or a colleague reached to pat his shoulder without warning. Because his nervous system constantly braced for sudden impacts, Amir found himself retreating into his own skull. He began pretending these violent encounters were happening to other therapists at conventions, carefully steering his thoughts away from the event while constantly scanning his own frame for new twinges of injury. Every unexpected jolt-the drop of a chart, the sudden turn of a partner in bed-ripped through him as if he were still backing into a wall, and because he could not trust his own reactions to make sense, he began to treat every familiar scent and every shift in physical proximity as an immediate threat, a feedback loop that tightened with every missed shift and every evening spent lying rigid beside his wife, his hand hovering over her arm but never landing. His belief that he was fundamentally damaged did not just spark alarm; it recalibrated his perception, ensuring that ordinary clinic interactions continued to detonate his startle response. The sheer frequency of these false alarms kept his nervous system in overdrive, ensuring that every familiar scent and every shift in physical proximity continued to register as an immediate threat. Avoiding the memory and dissociating from daily sensations meant that no safe experiences could overwrite the trauma, so ordinary cues continued to detonate his startle response, a minor but persistent static that barely registered beneath the louder machinery of his fear. Six months into his marriage, the silence in their bedroom had grown louder than the trauma itself. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, that any attempt at intimacy would only confirm his damage. The final push to seek treatment came when he dropped a sterile tray during a routine assessment, watching it scatter across the tile while his own heart hammered against his bruised ribs, realizing he was no longer capable of holding his patients or his own life together. He had come to the clinic not to dissect the past, but to find a way to stop flinching from a touch that meant care, hoping, against all his current evidence, to finally trust his own body again.
